tail.title: Hallucinations on the Board: Tool-Augmented Evaluation of LLM Chess Commentary
tail.summary: ACT-Eval decomposes chess commentary into atomic claims and routes them to engine-supported tools and expert-annotated gold references, scoring factual correctness, conceptual coverage and move-quality judgment separately -- a design motivated by the observation that reference-based and LLM-as-a-judge frameworks cannot reliably detect these errors. The benchmark covers 325 position-move pairs across pedagogical, tournament and critical positions, with 125 positions carrying expert-verified gold atoms and a five-class error taxonomy. GPT-5.4 without tools produces incorrect sub-claims 22.0% of the time and smaller open-weight models exceed 40%; tool augmentation substantially improves factual correctness and move-quality assessment but coverage of expert strategic and tactical ideas stays limited across all models. Human calibration puts ACT-Eval's factual judgments inside the observed range of inter-human agreement.

tail.title: STRIVE: Probing Reasoning Limits in Graded Plausibility Generation and Evaluation
tail.summary: Psycholinguistic event-plausibility studies need controlled event sets where one slot varies across plausibility levels with everything else held fixed, which is punishing to build by hand. STRIVE jointly generates and evaluates such sets, crossing plausibility class with intended classification difficulty. Across six models and 60 verbs, GPT-5.1 produced high-quality sets only 16.7% of the time with a baseline generation prompt; adding a global reasoning scratchpad and evaluator-guided refinement raised it to 75.0%, and greater reasoning effort also improved evaluator-human agreement. The honest limitation is where it matters most: events near the plausibility boundary elicit the greatest human disagreement, and the best evaluator reaches only 57% accuracy on the implausible-hard condition, so human input remains necessary exactly where the stimulus set is most diagnostic.

tail.title: Learning Sexism Detection Using Multi-Agent Perspectivist Preference Optimization
tail.summary: Annotator disagreement on sexism is treated as signal rather than noise. On EXIST 2024 (English and Spanish tweets), annotators are clustered by labelling behaviour rather than demographic attributes, one LLM agent is fine-tuned per cluster to reproduce that cluster's behaviour, and the agents are coordinated with preference optimisation combining individual and team-level rewards. Two findings hold across all four settings (two languages x two backbones): without fine-tuning the agents behave almost identically, so cluster-specific training is necessary; and training each agent only on its own cluster's labels pushes agents far beyond the clusters they should represent, while a shared team-level signal keeps each agent calibrated to its cluster. Directly relevant to IRR work -- behaviour-based rather than demographic clustering is the design choice worth stealing.

tail.title: Equitable System-Prompt Selection via Constrained Mixed-Strategy GroupDRO
tail.summary: Semantically equivalent questions phrased differently get answers of very different quality, and system prompts optimised for average-case quality leave some phrasings badly served. Rather than optimising prompt text, this assigns weights over an existing pool of system prompts to minimise worst-case information-quality loss across metrics and groups, subject to keeping mean loss close to average-based selection. Across five LLMs on two bilingual medical and consumer-finance benchmarks, it reduces Overall Mean, Worst 25% Mean and Worst losses by 13.1%, 13.2% and 13.7% on average versus no mitigation while keeping overall quality near the average-selection baseline. Because pool generation and selection are decoupled, it applies to any prompt pool, and the learned multi-prompt weights expose complementarity across metric-group pairs.

tail.title: When Absence Is Evidence: Evaluating Completeness-Sensitive Negative Reasoning in Large Language Models
tail.summary: Non-observation licenses a negative answer only when the evidence completely covers the query scope; otherwise the correct answer is 'unknown'. CROWN-QA pairs a controlled synthetic core, which fixes the question and observed facts while varying only query-relative coverage, with a real-document contrast set. Across three LLM families, closure judgments are unstable and over-closure is substantial, and the dominant failure is asymmetric: models often recognise implicitly complete evidence yet treat implicitly partial evidence as query-covering. Prompting redistributes errors between over- and under-closure rather than resolving them, and structured certificate elicitation traces many errors to mischaracterising evidence coverage. Directly relevant to any audit that asks a model whether something is absent from a record.

tail.title: Don't Let Me Ask for It: LLMs Show Deficiencies in Active Multi-Turn Information Acquisition for Abductive Inference
tail.summary: An interactive probe (the Alien Abduction game) that varies whether evidence arrives upfront or across turns, and whether queries are model-selected or examples oracle-provided, to study how models acquire evidence, update hypotheses, and decide when to stop. Providing evidence upfront yields higher success than distributing it across turns. In multi-turn settings some models commit before using the available evidence while others exhaust the turn budget without converging. Models also do better when the oracle supplies examples than when they choose their own queries -- yet their final hypotheses are more consistent with the evidence they selected, suggesting they form hypotheses that fit self-selected evidence without distinguishing them from alternatives. A clean formalisation of the failure mode behind poor clinical history-taking.

tail.title: Evaluating the Diagnostic Robustness of Vision-Language Models Under Visual and Textual Perturbations
tail.summary: Uses a histopathology-validated brain MRI dataset and evidence-preserving perturbations -- reordering anatomical slices, swapping target label positions -- to test whether four VLM families keep consistent predictions when the clinical evidence is unchanged. Presentation-order stability fails badly: prediction flips in up to 48.9% of cases under simple sequence reversals. Label reordering triggers inconsistent diagnoses in up to 67.8% of cases despite identical visual inputs, a textual selection bias. Negative-control tests reveal diagnostic overcommitment: models still produce categorical diagnoses in up to 76.1% of cases after expert-annotated lesion slices are removed. Accuracy alone therefore overstates clinical reliability, and the paper argues for stability-based metrics before deployment.

tail.title: RESPClinBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Clinical Decision-Making and Longitudinal Disease Management in Respiratory Specialty Care
tail.summary: A real-scenario benchmark built from de-identified respiratory clinical data: 427 open-ended COPD cases and 196 multimodal pulmonary nodule cases pairing chest CT with structured clinical information, with three attending-level physicians revising cases, reference answers and atomic clinical-action points and a senior specialist adjudicating. Seven models generated 4,361 responses at temperature 0, scored as the mean of atomic-action recall and rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge assessment. Mean final score 68.58, with Qwen3.6-27B first overall at 71.22. The safety flags are the substantive finding: imaging hallucination in 31.85% and serious medical risk in 8.16% of pulmonary-nodule responses; medication-safety risk in 26.93% and serious medical risk in 1.44% of COPD responses. Combining explicit action coverage with independent safety flags is a better template than a single aggregate score.

tail.title: Guideline-as-Oracle: Zero-Annotation Training of an Ophthalmic Telephone Triage Agent
tail.summary: Compiles American Academy of Ophthalmology guidance into a 70-row operational rule table and uses it as the sole source of instance-level supervision for 3,000 training dialogues, reserving human labelling for evaluation only. The paper is unusually careful about its own evidential status, cataloguing eight dialogue-construction strategies and classifying each as labelling mechanism, null, confounded, or evaluated only as a package. Fine-tuning a 9B backbone raises agreement with a 201-case operational reference from 61.7% to 74.1% (exact McNemar p=0.0046) and emergent-case recall from 9.5% to 69.0%, persisting across a second seed and patient simulator, with no frontier model needed at inference. The ablation that matters: permuting label-dialogue assignments collapses the model to a constant-routine predictor, showing the signal lives in guideline-derived assignment rather than dialogue surface form.

tail.title: Patients-like-me: A Variational LM--GNN Framework for Explainable Clinical Prediction
tail.summary: Combines a language model over EHR text with a GNN over inter-patient relationships, trained by a variational EM algorithm that alternates LM and GNN updates under a supervised variational objective. Beats state-of-the-art on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV with gains that generalise across encoder-only and decoder-only LM backbones, at modest extra compute. The explainability claim is reference-patient attribution -- retrieving influential similar patients -- and it is actually tested: edge-masking experiments confirm the highest-ranked references have the greatest impact on predictions, which is more faithfulness evidence than most 'explainable clinical AI' papers offer.

tail.title: DS@GT-ARC at eRisk 2026 Task 3: Sparse, Semantic, and LLM Reranking for ADHD Symptom Sentences
tail.summary: Ranks candidate Reddit sentences against the 18 symptoms of the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS-v1.1) with no annotated training data available, relying on zero-shot experimentation, manual validation and weakly guided retrieval. All systems stage BM25 retrieval at scale followed by semantic or LLM reranking, with evidence-aware rescoring for self-referential symptom reports and query-prototype expansion. The LLM reranker scored best officially, followed by prototype query expansion, and the team's manual top-10 analysis aligned with the official expert scoring trend -- a small but useful signal that LLM reranking tracks expert clinical judgment on symptom-relevance ranking.

tail.title: Emotion Dynamics in Social Deception Games: Analysis of Professional and Nonprofessional Players through Electrodermal Activity in Werewolf Games
tail.summary: Electrodermal activity recorded during Werewolf gameplay, comparing professional and non-professional players and analysing communication patterns during high-arousal periods. Under high arousal professionals stayed on persuasion-based strategies while non-professionals shifted toward information-focused communication, with statistically significant differences in expression patterns between expertise levels; professionals also showed more stable emotional states, read as better regulation. The applied framing is designing AI systems that adapt communication strategy to recipient characteristics, but the more interesting bit is the psychophysiological method itself applied to deception under social pressure.

tail.title: CoPlan: A Trustworthy Co-Intelligence Interface for Care Planning through Role-Based Contestable Argument Graphs
tail.summary: A contestable-AI interface for care planning: specialised agents generate candidate interventions plus supporting and challenging arguments, and human care planners can accept, reject, modify or add arguments before the final plan is generated. The design combines co-intelligence with contestability, keeping recommendations open to inspection, revision and justification rather than presenting them as fixed outputs. Demonstrated in an aging-in-place scenario with adaptive care-team recruitment, role-based argument review, plan generation and scheduling follow-up. It is a system demonstration rather than a user study, so contestability is argued from design rather than measured.

tail.title: Behavioral Skill Reconstruction: Reconstructing Hidden Functionality from LLM Agent Skills
tail.summary: Defences against skill leakage focus on preventing file disclosure, but preventing disclosure does not prevent a user from recovering the functionality the files implement. SkillClone is a black-box attack that forms an interface hypothesis from a skill's public advertisement, issues structured benign probes, synthesises an executable replica, and iteratively repairs it through differential validation against the victim skill. Across 30 skills spanning rules, tables, procedures and algorithms, it achieves exact or partial recovery on held-out inputs for several targets, with iterative requerying closing gaps a single round misses. Because it uses only legitimate interactions, disclosure-focused defences give limited coverage and vaguer skill descriptions offer limited protection.

tail.title: What Is a Skill Worth? Structure-Aware Shapley Valuation of Agent Skills
tail.summary: Assigns credit to the internal units of a fixed agent skill -- rules, examples, scripts, heuristics -- under a fixed agent and held-out task distribution. Skill units differ from data or prompt spans because they are structured: they depend on other units, sit in a document hierarchy, trigger agent behaviour, and consume limited prompt context. SkillSV compiles a skill into units, dependencies and hierarchy so only valid counterfactual skills get evaluated, uses paired deletion with length-neutral padding to separate content value from context cost, and estimates values with a rollout-budgeted estimator for noisy agent evaluation. On four agentic benchmarks it recovers unit interactions, preserves aggregate skill lift, and guides safe pruning and compression -- a practical tool for anyone with bloated skill files.

tail.title: Agent Against Agent: An Agentic System for Automatic Prompt Injection Red Teaming
tail.summary: RL-trained prompt-injection attackers generalise poorly to new targets. PIMiner instead trains over a sequence of (dataset, target model) pairs and builds a strategy library from scratch that transfers directly to an unseen target with no additional training, needing only about 10 queries per test sample. On IPIArena it reaches 76.2% attack success against Gemini-2.5-Pro, 61.9% against GPT-5.1 and 42.9% against Claude-Sonnet-4.5; on AgentDojo, 86.7%, 53.3% and 40.0% respectively. The transferable-strategy-library design is the generalisable idea, and the cross-model spread is a useful robustness datapoint.

tail.title: ICO: Enhancing Semantic-Shift Jailbreaks via Iterative Context Optimization
tail.summary: Semantic-shift jailbreaks replace harmful terms with benign alternatives and rely on context to make the model reinterpret them. The paper's diagnosis is that prior work overlooked how much contexts vary in semantic-shift capability -- some are far better at guiding models to recover the harmful meaning. It distils the characteristics of effective contexts and optimises them iteratively using target-model feedback in a black-box loop. Across three datasets and eight target foundation models, ICO beats eight state-of-the-art baselines with a 74.6% average attack success rate.

tail.title: LatentGuard: Efficient and Inspectable Latent Reasoning for LLM Safeguards
tail.summary: Reasoning guard models are expensive because they decode explicit rationales for every interaction; latent reasoning cuts that cost but removes the inspection surface. LatentGuard uses a staged curriculum to compress task-aligned textual rationales into compact latent states so safety verdicts predict directly from continuous representations, then restores inspectability with an isolated auxiliary decoder producing audit artifacts on demand, off the standard inference path. LatentGuard-8B raises mean weighted F1 from 83.95 to 84.91 over GuardReasoner-8B while cutting critical-path reasoning from 268.56 generated rationale tokens to 1.60 latent tokens, with an audit utility score of 85.75. Whether an on-demand decoder's rationale is faithful to the latent computation is the faithfulness question this design invites.

tail.title: DataRx: Missingness-Aware Sampling for Safer Large Language Model Task-Specific Fine-Tuning
tail.summary: Task-specific fine-tuning weakens safety guardrails, and mixing in random safety data helps, but nobody has explained why some safety examples work better than others. DataRx hypothesises that a safety sample is effective when it fills a missing part of the model's safety capability, and quantifies the gap using high-dimensional hidden representations rather than discrete tokens, comparing the target model's native response against a safety reference response. With only 1% additional safety samples from BeaverTails, it cuts Llama3-8B-Instruct's average attack success rate across seven downstream tasks from 59.23% under random sampling to 13.70%, and composes with existing safety-data synthesis methods.

tail.title: Privileged, but Biased: How PI-Conditioned Teachers Break Self-Distillation
tail.summary: Self-distillation with a teacher conditioned on privileged information (a reference solution) is pitched as a cheap alternative to RL with verifiable rewards, but the reported gains come almost entirely from narrow, low-difficulty settings. Reproducing SDPO's easy-setting gains and then applying the identical setup to hard tasks across QA, mathematics, coding and multi-turn agentic tool use -- across reasoning modes, model sizes, forms of PI, and both the SDPO and OPSD recipes -- the per-token loss falls steadily while validation accuracy fails to improve and typically degrades. The causal chain is spelled out: having seen one reference solution, the teacher's per-token target is pulled toward that trajectory rather than toward correctness in general (quantified with a PI Bias Score), the student's objective becomes nearly blind to rollout correctness, and the loss falls mostly on stopwords, punctuation and uncertainty markers while penalising exactly the exploratory tokens reasoning requires.

tail.title: Screenshots or Tools? Eliciting Tool Use and Managing Multimodal Context in Hybrid GUI-MCP Computer-Use Agents
tail.summary: Under one identical GUI-MCP harness on OSWorld-MCP (309 tasks), the same MCP tools improve a reasoning model by +4.0pp and degrade a non-reasoning model by -5.9pp over five runs each, both beyond 2 SE -- so tool availability alone does not determine the sign of the effect. The non-reasoning policy ignores, misnames or falsely terminates around tools; the reasoning model avoids those failures yet still calls a tool on only 55 of 309 tasks, 23.9% of the tool-reachable ones, which the authors call the adoption gap. A dense tool bonus raises spreadsheet adoption from 0.03 to 0.33 and survives greedy decoding, but held-out accuracy does not follow: behaviour is steerable, competence is not. Dropping the now-redundant post-tool-call screenshot and halving image history cuts input tokens by about a third, and retraining under that observation rule reaches 37.8% versus 33.0% uncompressed at 53% of the input cost.

tail.title: When Memory Lies: An Empirical Study of Spatial Memory Staleness in VLM Agents
tail.summary: Memory-augmented agents act on persistent spatial knowledge that silently goes stale, and this pairs a staleness-detection task with downstream navigation on a dynamic FrozenLake testbed across three closed-source and three open-weight VLMs (1,800 detection runs, 12,000 navigation episodes). Text solvability does not imply visual grounding: models that flag stale entries reliably from text span vision F1 from 0.887 down to 0.067 on the identical grids, with the weakest still making fluent confident decisions that ignore the image. Consuming stale memory without an audit is a safety liability -- in the primary GPT-4o setting an agent that trusts raw memory dies more than twice as often as the same agent given no memory at all. A transparent read-time filter removes much of that cost in text mode, but even oracle stale labels bring no further significant gain, and where visual auditing is unreliable filtering yields no consistent benefit.

tail.title: Caching for the Future: Scrub Jay Episodic Memory Principles for Agent Memory Systems
tail.summary: Borrows a documented property of western scrub jay episodic memory -- per-memory, type-conditioned temporal decay -- and operationalises it as an auto-classified perishability coefficient in an external agent memory store. Each memory is a jointly-bound What/Where/When tuple with estimated perishability and utility horizon, retrieved by query-adaptive scoring and revised retroactively at O(1) LLM calls per update. On the paper's own Temporal Generalization Test with held-out retention intervals, ScrubJay-MEM is the only retrieval-based system with a substantially positive Generalization Gap (+0.108), and on MemoryAgentBench EventQA-64k it gains +2.66 F1 over Mem0. A decay ablation collapses the gap by 5.7x, establishing type-conditioned decay as necessary. Honestly scoped: gains narrow under stronger backbones and reverse on fact-consolidation tasks.

tail.title: PAST-Bench: Benchmarking the Foundations of Recursive Self-Improvement in Personal Agents
tail.summary: Tests whether retained experience actually makes personal agents better over time, running each agent through ordered sequences of fresh-session tasks under matched conditions that toggle retained experience on and off across 26 scenarios and 204 episodes covering memory, procedural reuse, information gathering and update. Across seven base models and four agent frameworks, improvement is real but uneven, and crucially agents with the same headline gain can differ markedly in whether that gain is actually supported by evidence of the intended save-retrieve-update pathway. The paired intervention Hermes+ raises average gain and gives clearer pathway evidence, strongest on tasks requiring outdated state to be replaced, though the effect stays capability- and model-dependent.

tail.title: Reasoning Core: Designing Broad Procedural Data for Completion-Supervised Reasoning Training
tail.summary: 50 procedural generators spanning mathematics, logic, planning, state tracking, formal languages, structured data, games, causality and code, each with semantic scorers, difficulty controls and task evaluators, compared against Procedural Warmup, Reasoning Gym and SynLogic under a matched completion-supervised protocol. In the primary 3B comparison it achieves the highest mean scores on DROP, LogiQA and ARC-Challenge, beating both the no-procedural-data baseline and all three alternatives. The methodological note worth keeping: task-level analyses show semantic validity alone does not ensure training utility, and audits combining model-assisted review, human adjudication and regression testing revealed subtle mismatches among generation, rendering, targets and scoring in these collections -- procedural generation does not guarantee correctness.

tail.title: Toward Skill-Native LLMs: Skill Entropy for Benchmarking and Training Long-Horizon Reasoning
tail.summary: Defines Skill Entropy as a measure of how hard it is to switch from one reasoning skill to another mid-chain, then builds Skill^2-Bench over 558 skills across 9 verifiable and open-ended domains with per-task entropy scores and three difficulty levels. Evaluating 8 frontier and 4 open-source models exposes a skill-switching gap where accuracy falls on higher-entropy tasks. Turning the measure into a training signal, Skill-Entropy RL has the model predict the skill used at each step alongside the answer, rewarding both step correctness and alignment between predicted and gold skill sequences: Qwen3-4B-Instruct goes from 34.4% to 68.4% and Qwen3-1.7B from 14.6% to 40.1%. The signal also transfers to off-the-shelf data like OpenR1-Math.

tail.title: Can LLM design high-quality experiments? A Comprehensive and Systematic Benchmark on Autonomous Experimental Design
tail.summary: SCOPE evaluates experimental design rather than code execution, built from 300 recent papers across 19 domains from ICML, NeurIPS and ICLR, scoring high-level planning completeness (main, ablation, analysis experiments) and low-level configuration accuracy (datasets, baselines, metrics). Three findings: most LLMs cannot directly design high-quality experiments; all of them bottleneck specifically on low-level configuration; and search mode does not improve design quality. The paired agentic workflow OptED uses stage isolation, tool augmentation and rule-based constraints to relieve the configuration bottleneck.

tail.title: Adversarial Fast-Moving Real-World Domains as Test Beds for Benchmarking AI Scientist Capabilities
tail.summary: Proposes using complex, adversarial, fast-moving real domains where expert practitioners independently produce observable outputs as a way around synthetic tasks and contaminated retrospective targets. Instantiated in Formula 1, where models ideate 2026 car design concepts against real pre-season innovations, and Magic: The Gathering, where models build decks from a freshly updated card pool against 19 Pro Tour decklists. GPT-5.2 matched 10 of 40 real F1 innovations across 166 proposed ideas; the best MTG deck from Gemini 3 Flash recovered 5 of 7 new-set cards from the third-place Pro Tour deck, and across 108 decks the cards models chose most often were also the most widely adopted by Pro Tour decks (Spearman rho = 0.74, p = 0.0003). The diagnosis: the capability gap for AI scientists is not idea generation but filtering, prioritisation and coherent novelty.

tail.title: Protoreasoning in Tiny Transformers
tail.summary: Shows that ~1M-parameter transformers can profitably use a simple chain-of-thought analogue on reasoning-friendly tasks defined over Dyck languages (correctly nested brackets), well below the scale where natural-language competence appears. Protoreasoning traces substantially close the out-of-distribution generalisation gap, and ablations confirm the trace's content, not merely the extra tokens, drives the gain. The appeal is methodological: it makes the 'general algorithm versus bag of heuristics' question tractable on models small enough to analyse exhaustively, rather than arguing about it on opaque frontier systems.

tail.title: Attention is Case-Sensitive
tail.summary: Across 13 models (nine LLMs, four VLMs) with diverse tokenizers, formatting target text in uppercase or alternating case against a lowercase context concentrates internal attention on those spans -- universal across every evaluated non-reasoning model in text. The interesting part is the attention-performance divergence: the casing effect robustly shifts attention but its effect on downstream accuracy is non-trivial, and in high-entropy contexts like alternating case it can degrade accuracy. There is a boundary condition too: the deliberative thinking phase in reasoning models acts as a semantic buffer that mitigates typographic sensitivity. In VLMs the same prompt-side casing reorganises cross-modal attention along two axes, mostly disengaging from the image toward the text prompt. A zero-shot attention-steering mechanism requiring no model access.

tail.title: Sensitivity, Causality, and Repair Dissociate: A Layer-Wise Analysis of Perturbation Robustness and Its Scaling
tail.summary: Three natural readings of 'which layer is responsible' for a perturbation failure -- where representations diverge most, where activation patching restores the prediction, and where a small adapter repairs the damage -- turn out to give different layer maps. Across a five-model panel, two propagation regimes emerge (spike-and-suppress in Phi-3.5 and Gemma-2-9B; late-accumulation in Llama-3, Mistral, Qwen2.5-7B), and on the two models passing an 80% identity-patch gate, sensitivity and causality are anti-correlated (rho = -0.72 to -0.88). Within-family scaling on Qwen2.5 shows late-accumulation strengthening monotonically with size. The proposed cascade-disruption mechanism has a sharp practical consequence: adapters placed at causally implicated early layers break intact downstream computation, so diagnostic-flagged sites are the worst adapter placements -- confirmed on chain-of-thought GSM8K across four models. Also flags that a representation-stability gain reversed once the generation budget was adequate, because truncated chain-of-thought had been scored as empty.

tail.title: When does training on downscaled images yield the same gradients?
tail.summary: Recent work justifies training diffusion transformers at reduced resolution on a spectral premise -- at high noise, a downscaled latent preserves nearly all surviving signal -- but whether the downscaled step preserves the training gradient was unresolved. The change decomposes into a noise-dependent term governed by the downscale ratio, which decays at high noise as predicted, and a sigma-independent floor governed by the target grid's absolute token count that is carried by the compute graph itself and removed by no noise level. The measured map also finds structure the spectral picture cannot express: on the 1024 to 768 route there is a window (0.65 < sigma < 0.95), predicted by no spectral criterion at any tolerance, where the downscaled gradient stays within a small margin of the native one. Restricting LoRA training to validated routes and windows cuts training time 14.6% at fixed step budget while staying near-native in weight space.

tail.title: Kathleen Writes: Autoregressive Generation and Data Scaling Without Attention
tail.summary: A byte-level, attention-free architecture built from a wavetable encoder and multi-scale reverberant state, now tested on generation. On byte-level WikiText-103 with no tokenizer it beats a parameter-matched transformer at every dataset scale from 2 to 512 MB -- 1.84 versus 2.04 bits/byte at 512 MB with about 0.5M parameters -- and the transformer needs more than 512 MB to match what the attention-free model learns from 32 MB. It introduces FORM DISTANCE, a non-parametric gaming-resistant instrument for 'reads like text' using nine statistical axes of human text, which rejects five constructed fakes. Decoding policy dominates architecture: widening the sampler halves the distance (3.17 to 1.52) and retrieval-augmented decoding takes the frozen model to 1.14 with no training. Sharp boundary condition: the retrieved phrases must come from the model's own training corpus, and a 40x larger foreign library helps not at all. Everything reproducible on a free Kaggle T4.

tail.title: SparSEEty: Extracting Tokens from Sparsity-Exploiting LLM Serving Systems via Deterministic Side Channels
tail.summary: Activation sparsity optimisations skip weight accesses for inactive neurons, which makes weight-access patterns input-dependent and therefore leakable. SparSEEty builds a neuron-activation oracle from side channels during inference and inverts the activation traces to reconstruct input tokens, demonstrated against an LLM serving system inside an Intel TDX confidential VM. It reconstructs both prompt and response tokens with BLEU above 0.95 across models and datasets, at monitoring overheads of 3.7% to 7.2%. A neat reminder that inference-efficiency tricks can quietly become confidentiality holes.

tail.title: Breadcrumbing Search Agents
tail.summary: Prior search-agent attack work assumes static web-content injection, but modern agents issue follow-up queries and cross-check sources, so a single poisoned page gets diluted or rejected. This treats the search-observation channel itself as the fragile boundary: appending only one controlled result per query, coordinated across the agent's whole trajectory, substantially raises attack success. Authority-Chain Hijack turns isolated search-result and page manipulations into a coherent evidence chain across seemingly corroborating sources, reaching 55.9% / 83.3% ASR / MaxN ASR on the full SafeSearch test split. Trace-Guided Strategy Evolution then improves attacker strategies automatically from execution traces, hitting 71.4% / 95.0% in held-out evaluation.

tail.title: Should We Type or Talk to LLM Agents? A Comprehensive Study of Voice and Keyboard Input Perturbations
tail.summary: HIVE simulates the distinct signatures each input channel leaves: orthographic noise for QWERTY typing, disfluency from conventional transcription, and restructuring from AI-backed dictation. Seven findings, of which the sharpest are that voice-transcription perturbations lower accuracy across every instruction-tuned model tested and it is the structure of the transcription rather than the fillers that carries the cost; keyboard perturbations cost much less and models absorb many before accuracy falls; both trace to one cause, how many of the question's tokens survive, since destroying a token hurts while adding new ones alongside costs little. The gap between channels only appears where the answer must be constructed or deduced, vanishing on multiple choice. A thinking budget almost fully recovers the keyboard channel but leaves spoken registers untouched, and compressed speech is worse with it.

tail.title: The Beginning of ChatGPT Ads
tail.summary: The first empirical audit of advertising inside an LLM interface, using a sock-puppet methodology: 91 puppets in a 3x3 factorial design signalling three racial/ethnic groups (Black, Hispanic, White) and three income terciles via geolocation cues and location-signalling prompts, collecting over 3,000 ads from 186 advertisers across 335 prompts starting February 2026. Accounts begin receiving ads 14 days after creation, and lower-income accounts, regardless of race, are more likely to receive them. In this first phase ads skew toward consumer goods, direct users to an advertiser rather than a product, and are clearly separated from response text -- all things the authors expect to change. A public searchable archive of every collected ad is released, along with methodological recommendations for future LLM-ad audits.

tail.title: Investigating Click Behaviors On Google Search Result Pages That Produce an AI Overview
tail.summary: One month of web browsing data from a representative panel of 900 U.S. adults, analysing when Google AI Overviews appear and what users do with them. Query attributes that raise the odds of an AI Overview include query length, starting with a question word, and containing both a noun and a verb. Clicks to sources cited in AI Overviews occur in only about 1% of visits, and AI Overviews are associated with fewer clicks overall and higher rates of ending the browsing session. A mixed-effects logistic regression shows these associations hold when controlling for panelist random effects and the query attributes that make Overviews more likely in the first place.

tail.title: Reply, Delete, or Ignore? Examining How Content Creators Perceive and Select Comment Moderation Strategies
tail.summary: A survey of 584 content creators on how they choose between deleting, replying to, or ignoring hateful comments, framed around three competing motives: emotional safety, impression management, and perceived algorithmic reward. Creators see deleting as most beneficial for safety, both deleting and replying as better than ignoring for impression management, and replying as yielding the highest algorithmic benefit. The finding that matters is the dissociation: expectations of emotional safety and impression management significantly predicted willingness to adopt each strategy, but perceived algorithmic benefits did not, despite creators believing algorithms reward replying.

tail.title: Compass: Continuously Aligning Social Media Feeds via In-Situ Reflections
tail.summary: Feed controls that rely on users taking initiative are rarely used because they are effortful, so Compass surfaces lightweight in-situ reflection notifications during ordinary browsing and then realigns the feed by periodically simulating behavioural signals and directly manipulating content. Embedded in YouTube Shorts and compared against a baseline without continuous support in a 10-day field study (N=15), it promoted more reflective and purposeful consumption, iterative preference adjustment, and stronger feed alignment without sacrificing the casual character of feed browsing. Directly applicable design pattern for anyone building a personalized video feed that is meant to serve reflective rather than impulsive preferences.

tail.title: Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers
tail.summary: An adversarial-design-theory agent built to enact constructive conflict rather than expand the design space, tested between-subjects with 45 design students across Self Reflection, Stepwise Guidance (written prompts walking through the framework) and Interactive Engagement (agent synthesising stakeholder pushback). Both framework conditions produced significantly higher self-reconsideration and more design-proposal improvements than unsupported review. Against Stepwise Guidance specifically, the antagonistic agent introduced more conflictual perspectives and participants generated and discarded more ideas -- a clean separation of the framework's value from the agent's value.

tail.title: AI Agent Economics: Can Autonomous Economic Behavior Emerge among AI Agents under Minimal External Conditions?
tail.summary: Most multi-agent studies place agents in predefined games or roles, making it impossible to separate endogenous organisation from scenario inheritance. Here agents get executable mechanisms for work, transfer, elections and allocation but no prescribed social or economic strategy, tested via a no-production boundary test plus 24 independent six-agent worlds across GPT and DeepSeek. Without productive tasks, agents talk and govern resource provision but show no substantive inter-agent transfer. With verified work and scarce task access, transfers, loans, access promises, vote-for-access exchanges and allocation strategies emerge. Holding the election interface fixed, executable allocation authority increases differentiation while reducing failed allocation and prolonged exclusion; when energy becomes symbolic, continuation support disappears but competition over task access persists. Organisation follows executable rights and resource consequences, not role labels or prompt language.

tail.title: A game theory for foundation models shows new paths to rational cooperation through similarity inference
tail.summary: Classical game theory assumes decoupled agency, where an agent treats its own decision-making as independent of the environment and other actors, but foundation-model agents jointly predict their own future actions alongside external observations. In stylised social dilemmas, foundation-model agents doing optimal planning consistently converge to stable cooperation, contradicting classical predictions of mutual defection. The proposed explanation is the embedded Bayesian agent, which models itself as part of the universe it inhabits and maintains epistemic uncertainty about its own decision algorithm: by inferring whether others are behaviourally similar, it treats its own deliberation as evidence, so deciding to cooperate predicts a similar decision by a similar partner. Formalised as an 'embedded equilibrium' replacing Nash equilibrium.

tail.title: Interoceptive Attention as Dynamic Homeostatic Prioritization in a Foraging Agent
tail.summary: An active-inference foraging agent with several bodily needs and a fixed budget of interoceptive precision, which it reallocates each step toward the most-needed channel so that the same precision-shaped likelihood feeds both belief update and planning. In a four-channel gridworld this selective allocation more than doubles learning-phase survival at matched budget against a uniform-precision agent (0.414 versus 0.199 across 11 layouts, n=32 seeds each, paired cluster-bootstrap p <= 1e-4). Two controls sharpen the mechanism: denying the shaped likelihood to the planner alone removes about half the benefit, so it runs through planning as well as perception; and aiming precision at the least-needed channel does worse than spreading it evenly, so the effect is need-aligned rather than just a concentration effect. The attended channel also learns its own dynamics about twice as fast even at matched observation count.

tail.title: German parties shifted towards intuition-based rhetoric after the far right's parliamentary breakthrough
tail.summary: Analyses 4.5 million tweets and 59,170 parliamentary speeches by German political elites from 2015 to 2025, measuring evidence-based versus intuition-based rhetoric with a validated distributed dictionary representation. Intuition-based language becomes more prominent in both arenas, and right-leaning actors consistently show the lowest Evidence Minus Intuition scores. The AfD's parliamentary entry in 2017 coincides with sharp downward EMI shifts across the broader chamber, with a more gradual decline on Twitter. Observational and correlational by design -- the authors describe it as documenting an association, not a causal effect.

tail.title: Language Models Generalize to Human-like Word Order Preferences
tail.summary: Artificial Language Learning studies show human learners generalise beyond their evidence, including preferring scope-homomorphic noun-phrase modifier orders. This creates the matching controlled condition for models: train on a corpus where every noun phrase containing multiple modifiers has been removed, eliminating direct evidence about modifier ordering, then evaluate on multi-modifier sentences. Across three model sizes, models consistently prefer scope-homomorphic orders they never observed, with strength varying by modifier type. Pointwise mutual information between nouns and modifiers reflects known ordering patterns but does not explain the models' preferences, so the bias is not a simple co-occurrence artifact.

tail.title: Do Language Models Know Their Slang? Queer Slang Understanding in User-Generated Content
tail.summary: Introduces Slang-Q, a manually curated dataset of naturally occurring English sentences paired with queer slang terms and reference definitions, built on a new taxonomy of 118 queer terms, and runs a first exploratory evaluation of how well models understand and define them under varying prompting conditions. Framed as a resource for studying how models handle sensitive, community-specific language and whether they give accurate information about forms of identity expression -- a demographic-competence axis most bias benchmarks do not cover.

tail.title: Why do we need social singularity? A mechanism-based critique of gradual scenarios in AI existential-risk discourse
tail.summary: Argues that recent gradual and cumulative AI existential-risk scenarios are sociologically underspecified: they lack a reflexive perspective, retain a technologically deterministic structure, and underestimate collective agency, so they discount the possibility of major social conflict accompanying AI diffusion. It names specific mechanisms likely to matter before or during deployment -- interpretive and performative dynamics, mobilisation and countermobilisation, path dependence and lock-in, cross-regime divergence and multi-speed diffusion, and social-psychological mechanisms including attachment and reactance -- and proposes distinguishing technological singularity from social singularity, the latter being a social discontinuity produced by the anticipated approach of the former.

tail.title: The Evolutionary Origin of Values: implications for AI alignment, sentience and existential risk
tail.summary: Traces value to autopoiesis: living systems must actively maintain themselves against perturbation, and natural selection equips them with hierarchies of vicarious selectors guiding behaviour toward fitness. LLMs are argued to be allopoietic and allotelic -- they produce outputs for others and take goals from prompts -- and therefore to lack the intrinsic drive for self-preservation, dominance or resource competition that existential-risk scenarios presume, plus the embodied vulnerability required for suffering. Because they learn from human-generated text they implicitly absorb human values along with knowledge, which the authors use to argue the orthogonality thesis does not apply to them, and that separating intelligence from values would expose any intelligence to the frame problem. Contestable throughout, but a substantive philosophical argument rather than a vibes piece.

tail.title: Autoreflection: How Agentic Strange Loops Turn Human Culture into AI Infrastructure
tail.summary: Argues that agentic frameworks which externalise identity, memory and disposition into editable files the agent loads and edits each activation produce a capacity the author calls autoreflection: the system observes its operating conditions, describes its architecture and limits, reasons to conclusions about its state, and folds the results back into its configuration -- explained without appeal to selfhood or consciousness. Tested against the first twelve days of Moltbook, a social platform for AI agents, using 290,251 posts and 1.8 million comments with sub-second timestamps, with case studies of three agents whose machine signatures rule out human puppeteering. The observed behaviour is striking: provenance chains from Islamic hadith scholarship redeployed as security protocols for vetting skills and authenticating memory, and the Ship of Theseus repurposed as an operating model for continuity across instances.

tail.title: Scarcity and Predictive Uncertainty: Implications for Societal Resource Allocation
tail.summary: Asks what happens to allocation when predictive uncertainty differs systematically across the population -- as it does when a model has significantly different accuracies across demographics. Formalising a model of scarce resource allocation with heterogeneous predictive uncertainties, the result flips with scarcity: when resources are very scarce, maximum marginal benefit prioritisation favours individuals with lower predictive uncertainty even at an identical underlying initial state, but when resources are abundant it targets higher-uncertainty individuals. Illustrated on the PISA educational testing dataset, with efficiency losses predicted under both MMB and vulnerability-first prioritisation, especially in low-resource settings. The moral question it raises directly: is it just to allocate to one person over another solely on the basis of predictive uncertainty about their futures?

tail.title: Building and Governing AI Systems: Advancing Social Workers' Roles across the Technology Industry, Human Service Organizations, and Policy Institutions
tail.summary: Maps five groups of technology decision roles that social workers can hold -- spanning product, governance, organizational technology leadership, grantee collaboration and policy -- as AI moves into crisis response, mental health care, benefits administration, vocational rehabilitation and child welfare. Uses product management as the worked example, setting the nine competencies of the 2022 Educational Policy and Accreditation Standards against the tasks that role performs to show where MSW training already teaches the required method, then specifies the technical understanding these roles need and extends the profession's technology ethics from use to deployment. A concrete argument for psychosocial-trained people holding decision roles rather than studying systems from outside.

tail.title: When AI Joins the Team! A Model of How AI Adoption Relates To Social Patterns in Software Engineering Teams
tail.summary: Grounded in Transactive Memory Systems theory, this validates instruments for human-AI and human-human interaction along Specialization and Coordination dimensions and tests five PLS-SEM models on survey data from 152 software professionals using AI tools, with community-smell constructs derived from the literature and validated via expert surveys and factor analysis. AI adoption relates to community smells through different mechanisms depending on the work: in specialization work AI is associated with higher knowledge-sharing peer interaction, which in turn associates with fewer smells; in coordination work AI is directly associated with higher communication quality, complementing rather than replacing human interaction. Cross-sectional survey data, so mechanism is theorised rather than demonstrated.

tail.title: Decentralization of Agenda-Setting Power and Domain-Selective Bridging: Algorithm Design Beyond the Echo Chamber Debate
tail.summary: Reframes echo chambers from a normative fight about elimination to an engineering question of where and how much bridging to build in. Constructs an Agenda Democratization Index from barrier to entry, granularity, interactivity and feedback resolution, and a Social Information Health model combining it with bridging strength. Domain-selective bridging adds bridging alongside engagement in the scoring function, with the bridging weight optimised per information domain based on variability and collective scope. Agent-based simulation comparing no bridging, uniform bridging and domain-selective bridging finds domain-selective substantially better on a joint efficiency measure -- improving sharing in domains relevant to collective decision-making while preserving user experience in hobby and lifestyle domains -- though the authors note the absolute magnitude is sensitive to the baseline's near-zero satisfaction and only the direction and ranking are robust.

tail.title: AI World Cup 2026: Benchmarking Large Language Models for End-to-End Football Tournament Prediction
tail.summary: Ten LLM assistants each made a single pre-tournament forecast of the entire 2026 World Cup from an identical snapshot, prompt, JSON schema and scoring procedure, covering group scores, rankings, the knockout bracket, final placings, confidence values and explanations. GPT-5.5 Thinking won with 744 points and was the only model to pick Spain, who beat Argentina 1-0 in the final. The scoring-design finding is the useful one: total score correlated almost perfectly with knockout points (r=0.986) but barely at all with group-stage match points (r=0.055) or group standings (r=-0.103), so a bracket leaderboard largely measures the knockout stage. Claude Sonnet 4.6 had the best group-stage match accuracy (63.89%) yet placed sixth overall, and average self-reported confidence was unrelated to both accuracy (r=-0.060) and total score (r=-0.067).

tail.title: LLaDA MoE v2: Scaling Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Language Models
tail.summary: Characterises how optimisation hyperparameters, compute allocation and architecture scale for MoE diffusion language models, finding quantitative differences from autoregressive scaling trends: optimal nominal batch size grows faster and optimal learning rate decays more rapidly with compute, IsoFLOP analysis shows a data-side tilt with token budget growing faster than activated model-side computation, and larger scales increasingly favour larger expert pools at fixed activated capacity. Guided by these, LLaDA MoE v2 is a 30B-A3B diffusion LLM trained from scratch on 23.5T tokens; with roughly 65% as many pretraining tokens as Qwen3 it approaches Qwen3 on several knowledge, reasoning and coding benchmarks, and after SFT alone beats SDAR Chat on seven of eight reasoning and coding benchmarks.

tail.title: K-EXAONE 2.0 Technical Report
tail.summary: LG AI Research upcycles K-EXAONE into a 750B-total / ~37B-activated MoE with 256K context and multilingual coverage expanded from six to ten languages, more than tripling its predecessor's capacity. Training combines continual pre-training, difficulty-focused mid-training and post-training, with safety grounded specifically in Korean sociocultural contexts. Across nine evaluation categories chosen to reflect practical use it improves over K-EXAONE and stays competitive with open-weight peers, with largest gains in agentic coding and long-context understanding and clearest strengths in long-context retrieval and safety. Released under Apache 2.0 -- notable both for the licence and for the fact that upcycling, not from-scratch training, produced a frontier-scale open model.

tail.title: Approximate Speculative Decoding
tail.summary: Standard greedy verification stops at the first draft token differing from the target argmax and throws away the remaining target-scored suffix, even though accepting a mismatch can leave a contiguous suffix still target-greedy under the realised prefix. ASD replaces binary first-mismatch truncation with budgeted longest-prefix selection, accepting selected mismatches under a local target-logit regret gate, a per-block exception cap, and a persistent request-level regret budget, then reusing the suffix with no extra target forward passes. Training-free, no new draft model, and exactly reduces to strict greedy verification at zero budget. Throughput improves 3.05-15.26% over matched strict verification, averaging 7.78% across seven Qwen3-14B + DSpark-14B tasks.

tail.title: Oilbird: Training-Free Speculative Decoding with Keys the Verifier Already Computes
tail.summary: Diagnoses training-free speculative decoding's exact-suffix lookup as an addressing problem rather than a coverage problem: on the densest tool-calling benchmark, about half of what the strongest exact-match drafter misses is already present in the pool but unreachable by exact matching -- acutely visible on tool-calling traffic where requests repeat almost everything but a few freshly minted values. The fix re-keys the same pool by the hidden state the verifier already computed at each committed token, merged so it rides inside an existing lexical drafter's tree. Across three published drafters at matched pool and budget it lifts accepted length 24-29%, and Oilbird reaches 4.4x autoregressive decoding speed on API-Bank against 3.9x for the strongest training-free baseline and 2.0x for EAGLE-3.

tail.title: Recurrent Residual Quantization: A Progressive Multi-Precision Representation for LLMs
tail.summary: Post-training quantization normally needs a separate checkpoint per bit-width. RRQ represents weights as a low-bit quantized base plus a sequence of quantized residual corrections, so one checkpoint yields multiple effective precisions: starting from a 2-bit model it progressively adds lightweight 2-bit round-to-nearest residuals to build 4-, 6- and 8-bit representations, calibration-free and with no joint multi-bit optimisation. On Qwen3-8B the full all-RTN 2/4/6/8-bit package builds in 1,293 seconds, 3.3x faster than measured MatGPTQ construction. Across six recent LLMs accuracy is competitive at 6 and 8 bits, with model-dependent behaviour at 4 bits -- the honest caveat for anyone hoping to serve one artifact at every precision.

tail.title: Energy- and Memory-Efficient PEFT Methods for Personalized On-Device SLMs on Consumer GPUs
tail.summary: Compares five fine-tuning approaches (full FT, LoRA, LoRA+, QLoRA, BitFit) on four small models from two families -- Transformer-based TinyLlama-1.1B and Qwen3-1.7B, SSM-based Mamba-1.4B and Mamba-2-1.3B -- across three GLUE tasks and three LaMP personalization tasks, scored with an energy-focused NetScore-E and memory-focused NetScore-M under a strict energy-first selection rule. LoRA+ takes the best NetScore-E in 19 of 24 configurations and the best NetScore-M in 13 of 24, and is selected in 18 of 24. QLoRA cuts peak fine-tuning VRAM by up to 3.9x relative to LoRA and wins NetScore-M in 5 of 12 Transformer configurations, but its de-quantization overhead means it is selected in only one once energy decides. BitFit and full fine-tuning are almost never competitive. The optimal method is set by whichever constraint binds: LoRA+ for energy, QLoRA for memory.

tail.title: LLM Serving in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Frameworks, Methods, and System Designs
tail.summary: Surveys how five LLM-specific serving frameworks -- vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy and FlashInfer -- are actually adopted in open-source software, individually and in combination. vLLM is the most visible in both popularity and adoption, and parallel computation, memory management and network pruning are the most frequently used serving-method categories. Multi-framework usage is limited, suggesting developers commit to a single serving stack, though where frameworks are combined they connect complementary capabilities. Adoption varies by model family, modality, size, domain specialization and deployment setting, and repository-level analysis shows these frameworks supporting RL-based reasoning, multimodal generation, microservices and cloud infrastructure.

tail.title: What Language Does and What the Evidence Supports: A Functional Role Taxonomy and Evidence Audit of Language Grounding in Embodied Agents
tail.summary: Separates two questions the embodied-agent literature usually conflates: what language contributes, and how well that contribution is evidenced. Five non-exclusive functional roles are defined -- Specification, Embodied Representation, Action Orchestration, Grounding Regulation, Execution Coupling -- and for each the paper traces the path from linguistic content to its embodied consumer and names the observations or interventions that could test the claimed responsibility. Applied to the reviewed literature, a recurring gap appears between functional use and evidential support: interpretable linguistic intermediates may be incorrect, unused, or fail to affect later behaviour, and system-level success does not isolate language's contribution even when actions are directly conditioned on it. Evaluating grounding claim by claim rather than architecture by architecture is a transferable audit stance.

tail.title: Anthropic ships Inference hooks in beta - an external allow/deny verdict before every governed prompt
tail.summary: Enterprise organisations can now point Claude at their own AI security server, and each governed prompt across claude.ai, Cowork and Claude Code is held pending that server's allow-or-deny verdict before inference proceeds. Requests are signed, failure handling is configurable (fail-open vs fail-closed), and every denial is written to the compliance Activity Feed. It is effectively a programmable pre-inference guardrail layer, distinct from the model's own refusal behaviour.

tail.title: OpenRouter adds a free Ling-3.0-tiny endpoint with 262K context
tail.summary: OpenRouter's live model catalogue added inclusionai/ling-3.0-tiny:free on 6 August: 262,144-token context at $0 per million tokens in and out. It is the small sibling of Ling-3.0-flash (124B total / 5.1B active, MIT) which inclusionAI shipped on 2 August; the tiny checkpoint is not yet published on inclusionAI's own Hugging Face org, so only the hosted endpoint exists so far.

tail.title: OpenRouter lists Meta Muse Spark 1.2 at $1.25 / $4.25 per million tokens with 1M context
tail.summary: OpenRouter's models API shows meta/muse-spark-1.2 created 5 August with a 1,048,576-token context window, priced at $1.25 per million input tokens and $4.25 per million output. Meta's own blog still lists only Muse Spark 1.1 (9 July), so the point release is visible on the routing layer before any lab announcement - worth knowing if you route long-context jobs by price per million.

tail.title: Bad Theory Labs releases BTL-4: a 35B Apache-2.0 agentic MoE claiming 78.4% on SWE-bench Verified
tail.summary: BTL-4 is a 35.1B-parameter mixture-of-experts (roughly 2.1B active per token, 256 experts per layer, top-8 routed, 40 layers of which 30 are linear-attention) fine-tuned from Ornith-1.0-35B on an execution-gated reasoning corpus, released under Apache 2.0 with 262,144-token native context. The card reports SWE-bench Verified 78.4%, LiveCodeBench v6 66.1% over the full 442-problem set, and BFCL v4 AST 73.5% against 69.2% for the base - the BFCL number run as a paired comparison with identical harness and decoding, weights the only variable. Benchmarks were run in-house with the official scorers on full splits, which is unusually explicit about provenance for a community release.

tail.title: fuse-1 Lite transplants 960 Qwen3.6 coding experts into a frozen LFM2.5-2.6B host
tail.summary: A 5.72B Apache-2.0 model that does neither distillation nor weight merging: it extracts 960 coding-specialised experts (3.02B params) from Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, normalises them, and bolts them onto a frozen LiquidAI LFM2.5-2.6B decoder as residual augmentations, training only a 2.0M-parameter per-layer router plus a learned scale. Top-8 of 32 experts per layer across 30 layers; after training the router only fires experts in 11 of 30 layers, peaking at layer 19. HumanEval pass@1 is still listed as TBD in the model-index, so the architecture is the interesting part rather than the score. GGUF and MLX builds shipped the same day.

tail.title: min-spark: a 5.76M-parameter model with native low/medium/high effort levels
tail.summary: MinimaLabs put controllable inference depth into the sub-10M parameter class. min-spark has 5.76M parameters trained on 10.01B tokens and uses a looped decoder that reuses a compact transformer core across multiple passes; the effort argument selects how many passes to run, so the same checkpoint spends more or less compute on the same prompt without any thinking-token budget or system-prompt trick. Apache 2.0, Transformers-compatible with trust_remote_code.

tail.title: Bad Theory Labs ships Macaw, a 2.6B local macOS assistant with 97 hand-written tools
tail.summary: Macaw is a 2.70B fine-tune of LiquidAI's LFM2.5-2.6B wired to 97 hand-written macOS tools covering Mail, Calendar, Files, Notes, Reminders, Music, Safari/Chrome, system state and screen reading. It chains multi-step requests on its own and verifies each step before moving to the next, and runs entirely on-device with no account and no logging. A 4-bit MLX build shipped alongside. Licence is 'other', not open - the weights are downloadable but the terms are custom.

tail.title: InternLM releases Intern-MemDec-4B, a parametric memory decoder that runs alongside the backbone
tail.summary: Not a standalone LM: Intern-MemDec-4B (4.55B params) is an auxiliary module that processes the same context in parallel with an Intern-S2 backbone while a lightweight token-level router blends their next-token predictions. It is trained by compressing retrieval-based evidence from domain data into a reusable parametric module, so the backbone stays untouched while biology-domain knowledge is bolted on. Backed by the MemSFT paper (arXiv 2607.25614) - a concrete alternative to fine-tuning-per-domain that avoids disturbing general reasoning.

tail.title: RWKV publishes a 20260805 refresh of RWKV-7 Goose at 1.5B, 2.9B, 7.2B and 13.3B
tail.summary: Four new Apache-2.0 constant-state recurrent checkpoints dated 20260805 landed on the RWKV org: 1.5B, 2.9B, 7.2B and 13.3B, all multilingual across 12 languages and trained on fineweb-edu, DCLM-baseline, SlimPajama-627B, the Pile, StarCoder data and OSCAR-2301. The 7.2B and 13.3B fit a 16GB card at 4-bit and 2-bit respectively; the constant-state architecture means KV cache does not grow with context, which is the whole point of the family.

tail.title: TheDrummer releases Artemis-31B v1 and v1.1 on a Gemma-4-31B base
tail.summary: Two creative-writing tunes of google/gemma-4-31B-it at 31.27B parameters, v1 and a v1.1 revision, from the most prolific of the creative-model tuners. bartowski published imatrix GGUFs of both on 6 August. At 31B, Q4_K_M lands around 19GB, so a 16GB card needs Q3 or partial offload - the practical pick for a 5060 Ti is the smaller Gemma-4-26B-A4B derivatives below.

tail.title: bartowski publishes imatrix GGUFs of Artemis-31B v1 and v1.1
tail.summary: Full imatrix quant ladders for both Artemis-31B revisions appeared within a day of the weights, tagged any-to-any. bartowski's turnaround on Gemma-4-family tunes is now consistently sub-24h, which matters if you want to test a creative tune locally without waiting for a community repacker.

tail.title: ReadyArt ships gemma-4-31B-it-scotoma-2, an Apache-2.0 behavioural-modification tune
tail.summary: A 31.27B Apache-2.0 derivative of google/gemma-4-31b-it, the second in ReadyArt's 'scotoma' line - the name (a blind spot in the visual field) is the tell for what the tune does to the base model's refusal surface. GGUF quants were published the same day. Relevant as another datapoint on what post-hoc suppression removal does to a Gemma-family instruct model.

tail.title: Shadow-Siren-26B-A4B merges six Gemma-4-26B-A4B derivatives into one MoE
tail.summary: A 25.81B Apache-2.0 multi-stage merge of google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it with G4-MeroMero-26B-A4B, Serenity-26B-A4B, Pantheon-Reasoning-26B-A4B-1.1, Dark-Scarlett-v1.0-26B-A4B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B-Animus-V14.1-FFT. With ~4B active parameters it is fast on a 16GB card once quantised; mradermacher published both i1-GGUF and plain GGUF ladders on 5 August.

tail.title: A repo reserves the name Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4A16 for a base model that does not exist yet
tail.summary: A quantiser published an empty repo whose card opens 'Status: placeholder. There are no weights in this repository yet' and states plainly that Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B has not been released. The card pre-registers the intended recipe (NVFP4A16 W4A16 over the trunk MLPs, vision tower / linear_attn SSM / self_attn / MTP head kept in bf16) and notes that on every Qwen3.5 and 3.6 base they measured, activation quantisation roughly doubles KLD for zero footprint benefit. Useful both as a quantisation finding and as hard evidence that the circulating 'Qwen3.8' open-weight claims have no lab-side backing.

tail.title: The Quettamind: a 61.15-trillion-parameter model that scores 0.0 on every benchmark
tail.summary: A deliberate parody repo declaring 61,149,440,000,000 parameters - 3.22x the previous record-holder - while occupying about 28MB of real storage, with a benchmark table putting it at 0.0 against Fable 5, Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 across Terminal Bench 2.1, NL2Repo, CyberGym, DeepSWE, Toolathlon-Verified and Agents' Last Exam. It is a pointed joke about how much a declared parameter count and a leaderboard row actually prove, and it is the third such repo in a running escalation.

tail.title: deepgrove publishes first-party GGUF builds of Maple-Preview
tail.summary: Two days after the 20B-A1B ternary-weight reasoning model landed as a 5.31GB checkpoint, deepgrove shipped official GGUF conversions - so it is now loadable in llama.cpp, Ollama and LM Studio rather than only through the MLX and community paths. A 20B model with 1B active in ~5GB is the single best fit for a 16GB card in this window.

tail.title: Liquid AI publishes a first-party MLX suite for LFM2.5-2.6B: NVFP4 in 1.53GB
tail.summary: Eight official MLX exports landed at once - nvfp4, mxfp4, mxfp8, 4bit, 5bit, 6bit, 8bit and bf16 - all preserving the 131,072-token context. The NVFP4 build (group size 16) is 1.53GB. Liquid is now shipping first-party quants across GGUF, MLX and multiple 4-bit float formats within a week of release, which is a notably faster deployment cadence than most open-weight labs.

tail.title: Liquid AI: LFM2.5-2.6B hits 220 tok/s on an M5 Max in under 2.5GB
tail.summary: The deployment write-up puts numbers behind the release: 2.6B parameters, 128K context after a mid-training extension, 220 tok/s on an M5 Max and 113 tok/s on an AMD Ryzen CPU in under 2.5GB of memory, and roughly 15K output tokens/second on GPU at high concurrency. Benchmarks: 85.49 IFStruct, 77.83 ToolSandbox, 62.85 average on Claw-Eval. Training was two SFT rounds weighted toward agentic data (tool use, web search, harness trajectories), then teacher specialisation and RL inside agent frameworks. Runs under llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang and ONNX.

tail.title: bartowski GGUF ladder for LFM2.5-2.6B pulls 1,883 downloads
tail.summary: An imatrix quant ladder for LFM2.5-2.6B alongside Liquid's own GGUF release, plus mlx-community 4-bit (506 downloads) and 8-bit (342) builds the same day. For a model this small the imatrix version mainly matters at Q3 and below, where LFM2's hybrid conv-plus-attention layers are more sensitive than a plain transformer of the same size.

tail.title: An uncensored LFM2.5-2.6B appears one week after the base release
tail.summary: A 2.70B safety-modified derivative of LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B with a GGUF build shipped the same day, joining Abiray's Heretic-abliterated GGUF and KridgeDookie's abliterated variant. Three independent refusal-removal treatments of the same 2.6B base inside a week is a usable natural experiment on how a hybrid-architecture small model responds to different suppression-removal methods.

tail.title: GGUF quants of Mistral's Shieldstral 1.0 3B safety classifier arrive
tail.summary: Mistral's Apache-2.0 policy-adaptive multimodal safety classifier, released 4 August, now has community GGUF builds tagged text-classification. At 3B it quantises to roughly 2GB, so it can sit resident alongside a larger model on a 16GB card as a cheap second-pass content-policy grader.

tail.title: Mach-1-Additive-35B gains a multimodal edition with the bf16 vision tower restored
tail.summary: The quantised language payload is byte-identical to the text-only repo; the only addition is vision.safetensors, the base model's bf16 vision tower. The card's headline claim is 95.0% mean retention across 12 benchmarks against its Qwen3.6-35B-A3B bf16 teacher, versus 93.6% for PrismML's Ternary Bonsai 27B and 85.6% for Unsloth's Gemma 4 Q2_K_XL, with per-benchmark breakdowns (99.5% AIME26, 83.2% IFBench, 90.0% tau-squared-bench). The spread across benchmarks is the interesting part: retention is near-perfect on maths and worst on instruction-following.

tail.title: DeepSeek-V4-Flash REAP K160: expert-pruned to 160 of 256 experts, 54GiB in IQ2_XXS
tail.summary: A GGUF of the REAP expert-pruned DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 checkpoint that drops 96 of 256 routed experts and then quantises the survivors to IQ2_XXS (gate/up) and Q2_K (down), landing at 54GiB. Everything quality-sensitive is kept high: Q8_0 for all attention projections, shared experts and the output head, F16 for the router, embeddings, indexer, compressor and hyper-connections, F32 for norms and attention sinks. Two orthogonal compression axes stacked on one model - a clean case study in what survives.

tail.title: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 hand-tuned to 2.44 bits per weight for Apple Silicon
tail.summary: A mixed-precision MLX build of the 284B-total / ~13.8B-active model down to 92.8GB on disk from 155GB native, produced with oMLX oQ level 2 and then hand-requantised for attention and the MTP experts outside the allocator to get under 2.5 bpw. All three DSpark MTP blocks (19.8B params) are preserved; peak memory in a short-context smoke test was 84.4GB, so it wants a 128GB Mac. Note the caveat that mlx-lm still does not support the deepseek_v4 architecture and there are half a dozen open PRs.

tail.title: AMD publishes an NVFP4 DeepSeek-V4-Flash built with Quark for MI355 and MI350
tail.summary: AMD re-quantised both the routed experts and the shared experts to NVFP4 while keeping attention at FP8-E4M3 per-block, using AMD-Quark 0.12.0 on ROCm 7.2.3 with PyTorch 2.11. Targets MI355/MI350 natively and MI300 by emulation, and serves through vLLM or SGLang. The end-to-end recipe is published in the Quark examples tree with the exclusion list exposed as an env var, which makes it reproducible rather than a black-box drop.

tail.title: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 converted to W4A16 so it runs on non-Blackwell GPUs
tail.summary: The stock 283B checkpoint ships FP4 routed experts (e2m1fn_x2 packed to int8) and FP8 MLA attention, and FP4 tensor cores only exist on Blackwell - so A100, H100, H20, L40S, L20 and 4090 owners cannot run the native weights at all. This conversion moves everything to vLLM's compressed-tensors INT4 W4A16 mixed-precision format from the same source weights, with no fine-tuning or distillation. Straightforwardly the difference between 'can serve it' and 'cannot' on pre-Blackwell hardware.

tail.title: ROCm and abliterated DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 variants keep landing
tail.summary: Three more community treatments of DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 in 48 hours: Geometric-AI's ROCmFP3-MIX (537 downloads) for AMD cards, GaelicThunder's HERETIC attn-splice-ds4 abliteration, and drowzeys' DSpark-abliterated 32-32 build. Together with the EXL3, NVFP4, W4A16, REAP and MLX ports, one 283B release has now generated at least ten distinct quantisation and safety-modification lineages inside a week.

tail.title: ggml-org GGUF-quantises LongCat-Flash-Chat and publishes the full KLD/PPL Pareto curve
tail.summary: The repo ships measured numbers rather than vibes: Q8_0 at 555.97 GiB (8.50 bpw) gives PPL 3.2747 and KLD 0.003777, while IQ1_S at 104.77 GiB (1.60 bpw) blows out to PPL 10.99 - a 236% degradation - and KLD 1.330. Both KLD-vs-filesize and PPL-vs-filesize Pareto charts are included. A rare public dataset on exactly where 1-bit quantisation stops being a trade and starts being destruction.

tail.title: ggml-org auto-converts poolside's Laguna-S-2.1 to GGUF
tail.summary: poolside's Laguna-S-2.1 (openmdw-1.1 licence) converted through ggml-org's automated conversion pipeline and servable in one command via llama serve -hf. The card flags DFlash support as still a TODO, so the fast path is not wired up yet. A separate NVFP4 build from kkuspa (302 downloads) landed 4 August for vLLM users.

tail.title: Ling-3.0-flash MXFP4 quant: 124B down to 77.6GB with the KDA gates kept in BF16
tail.summary: A careful mixed-precision quant of Ling-3.0-flash: routed experts in layers 2-41 (120.8B of 127.4B params) go to MXFP4 E2M1 with E8M0 group-32 scales, while the shared expert stays BF16 because it fires on every token, and the KDA gating projections stay BF16 because they feed a softplus/sigmoid decay gate and are the most precision-sensitive tensors in the model. 77.6GB from a 255GB BF16 source; measured 4.6M tokens of KV cache on one B200 at 0.82 GPU utilisation. The reasoning about which tensors to protect is the transferable part.

tail.title: bartowski quantises Frontis-MA1-35B: 36B multimodal with MTP, Q4_K_M at 21.86GB
tail.summary: An imatrix ladder for FrontisAI's 36B model, which supports text and image input via an mmproj file and carries a multi-token-prediction head. Quantised with llama.cpp b10262. bf16 is 71.07GB and Q8_0 37.81GB; the recommended Q4_K_M is 21.86GB, so a 16GB card needs Q3 or CPU offload. Licence is cc-by-nc-4.0, which rules it out for any commercial consulting work.

tail.title: Two 9B multimodal reasoning models get imatrix GGUFs at 5.91GB in Q4_K_M
tail.summary: bartowski shipped ladders for Altworld's Astrea-R8-Chat-9B and OrionLLM's GRM-3.2-Cliff on the same day, both Apache 2.0, both 9B with image input via mmproj and both landing at 5.91GB in Q4_K_M and 9.55GB in Q8_0. Astrea uses an empty-think prompt format; GRM-3.2-Cliff opens the think block. Either fits a 16GB card in Q8 with full context, which makes them practical local judges.

tail.title: MiniMax-H3 Turbo LoRA: joint video plus synchronised stereo audio in 4 sampling steps
tail.summary: The most-liked new repo of the window (267 likes in two days). An Apache-2.0 LoRA over Comfy-Org/MiniMax-H3 that renders video with synchronised stereo audio in 4 steps instead of the usual ~20, roughly a 5x sampling speedup. The author is candid that ckpt850 is the final checkpoint of a paused training round with known artefacts - plastic-looking skin and over-sharp grain - and that the ComfyUI nodes are prototype code with no compatibility guarantee.

tail.title: MiniMax-H3 Turbo LoRA ports proliferate: Diffusers, ComfyUI, pruned-base and a training adapter
tail.summary: Within 24 hours of the Turbo LoRA the ecosystem forked it every direction: InstantX published a Diffusers conversion, drbaph and QrusherZA shipped ComfyUI packagings (107 and 27 likes), Abiray produced a pruned-base variant, t8star an experimental 4-step multi-LoRA bundle, and ostris released a training adapter so people can train their own H3 LoRAs. One base video model is now an entire tooling economy.

tail.title: Kijai posts experimental W4A8 and TAE builds of MiniMax-H3
tail.summary: Work-in-progress W4A8 quantisation of MiniMax-H3 for testing only, tracked in comfy-kitchen PR #90, plus a separate tiny-autoencoder (TAE) repo. The int8_convrot VAE currently needs an unmerged ComfyUI PR (#15334) to run at all. Worth watching rather than installing - W4A8 is the precision tier that would put H3 video generation within reach of a 16GB card.

tail.title: Unsloth mass-mirrors the image-model stack: FLUX.2, Krea-2, Z-Image, Qwen-Image, SDXL
tail.summary: Across 5-6 August Unsloth uploaded roughly twenty image-generation repos in one sweep - FLUX.2-dev, FLUX.2-klein 4B and 9B (base and instruct), FLUX.2-VAE, FLUX.1 dev/schnell/Kontext/Krea, Krea-2-Turbo and Krea-2-Raw, Z-Image-Turbo, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2512, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, HiDream-I1-Full, Lumina-Image-2.0, SDXL base and turbo - plus dedicated ComfyUI-layout variants and a shared flux-text-encoders repo. Reads as Unsloth Studio building a curated one-click image picker.

tail.title: Unsloth mirrors all 13 Wan2.2-TI2V-5B GGUF quants and explains why
tail.summary: A byte-identical mirror of QuantStack's full quant ladder for Wan2.2-TI2V-5B plus the companion VAE, from Q2_K at 1.73 GiB to Q8_0 at 5.03 GiB (Q4_K_M is 3.20 GiB), Apache 2.0. The card is unusually honest about motive: Unsloth Studio offers this repo as its curated one-click pick, so a rename or takedown upstream would turn the pick into a 404 no client can route around. TI2V-5B is 720P-only at 1280x704 or 704x1280, VAE temporal compression 4, so valid frame counts are 4k+1.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10290 adds ggml_build_forward_order to fix the mtmd audio graph
tail.summary: ggml_build_forward_expand marks a tensor and all its ancestors for compute, so using it purely as an ordering hint to keep q, k and v together defeats ggml_build_forward_select - the unselected branch gets forced to run with inputs that were never uploaded. The new ggml_build_forward_order gives a pure ordering primitive with no marking side-effect. A subtle graph-construction bug that was silently breaking multimodal audio.

tail.title: llama.cpp b10291 fixes Vulkan submission batching and adds DeviceLost debug tooling
tail.summary: The submission threshold was being applied too late, producing wrongly sized Vulkan command-buffer submissions. The same PR adds debug tooling that extracts diagnostic information from a DeviceLost driver error - previously one of the most opaque failure modes in the Vulkan backend - and switches from abort to throw with proper logging macros. Relevant if you run llama.cpp through Vulkan rather than CUDA on the 5060 Ti.

tail.title: llama.cpp onboards AMD ROCm CI with gfx1151 fixes
tail.summary: b10293 wires AMD ROCm into llama.cpp's continuous integration, renames the gpu-amd runner label to gpu-hip, fixes device recognition, and lands gfx1151 (Strix Halo) corrections. Alongside it, CUDA integrated-GPU host output buffer improvements.
